elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Inserted operative text: "Termination for Convenience by IBM. IBM may terminate this Agreement for its convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to MSL..." IBM is Customer; the element is disjunctive (Agreement or Order Form), and Agreement-level coverage satisfies it. The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present: false" is a false negative — it appears keyed to the literal alias "Customer", whereas the rendered clause uses the defined party name "IBM"; in substance the right is expressly granted.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to MSL" — exactly 30 days, in writing, and no additional conditions, approvals, or windows are attached.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "in which case MSL shall refund to IBM, on a pro rata basis, any fees prepaid by IBM for the period after the effective date of termination." The refund is expressly "on a pro rata basis" (not merely inferred from post-termination coverage), is payable by Vendor (MSL), and is triggered by the convenience termination.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Retained Section 5.0 opens "Notwithstanding anything in this Agreement to the contrary, this Agreement may be terminated by either Party for cause as follows:" — the only mid-term exits enumerated are for cause. The six/twelve-month notice rights in the term clauses operate as "unless" carve-outs to automatic renewal ("will automatically be renewed ... unless either Party gives six (6) months written notice"), i.e. natural-term non-renewal, which is assessed under RENEWAL rather than as mid-term T4C. § 6.1 gives cancellation rights to IBM (Customer), not MSL, so it does not create a Vendor convenience exit.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The inserted right runs on "thirty (30) days' prior written notice", which is below the 60–90 day fallback band. This is a deliberate preferred-level (Customer-favourable) result, not a defect; the fallback simply is not the level achieved.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the inserted clause imposes no early-termination fee or penalty on IBM for Agreement-level convenience termination, and no retained Section 5.0 formula attaches one. The § 6.1 cost reimbursements attach only to Purchase Order cancellation, not to the new Agreement-level right, so no capped fee is required.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: MSL has no express convenience right (Section 5.0 exits are for cause only), which is better than the fallback. However, the retained auto-renewal sentences ("unless either Party gives six (6) months written notice of its intent to terminate this Agreement"; twelve (12) months in the SOW Attachment) do not expressly tie the termination effective date to the end of the then-current term, so term-end-only cannot be affirmatively confirmed from the operative wording. Immaterial here because the fallback level is not the level relied on.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply in substance: MSL has no convenience termination right; and the only notice mechanic available to MSL (six months under the Base Agreement, twelve months under the SOW Attachment) exceeds 90 days in any event.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: all four preferred elements are met on the rendered operative language (30-day Customer convenience right, express pro-rata refund of prepaid fees, and no Vendor mid-term convenience exit).

The deterministic signal "Customer convenience termination present: false" is a mechanical false negative — the clause names the party by its defined term "IBM" rather than the alias "Customer". Inspected in substance, the operative sentence squarely grants the Customer convenience right, so the failed regex does not defeat the finding.

Minimality holds: the change is a single concise insertion into Section 5.0 with no deletions, no paraphrase of surrounding text, and no extras — it correctly omits "in whole or in part" (surplus absent a partial-termination/Order Form need) and adds no survival tail, expense allocation, transition, or procedural boilerplate.

Intent preserved: the insertion sits inside Section 5.0, so the term clause's "unless terminated as provided in Section 5.0" continues to operate without a dangling cross-reference; the for-cause mechanics, renewal notice periods, and § 6.1 Purchase Order cancellation/cost-reimbursement economics are untouched and not contradicted (the "Notwithstanding ... for cause" preamble is permissive, not an exclusive-remedy limitation).

The "deviation" status is correct: before the edit, a three-year committed term gave IBM no convenience exit at all, which the playbook treats as a deviation in any term longer than 12 months; the six/twelve-month notices are renewal-blocking and belong under RENEWAL.

Optional hardening (not required for completeness): if you want to foreclose any argument that Section 5.0's "Notwithstanding anything in this Agreement to the contrary ... for cause" preamble overrides the new clause, add "Notwithstanding Section 5.1," or renumber the insertion as a new Section 5.x expressly cross-referenced in the term sentence. As drafted this is not a defect, since the preamble does not say termination may occur "only" for cause.

Optional hardening: if IBM wants the exit to reach individual Purchase Orders/Order Forms as well as the Agreement, extend the clause to "this Agreement or any Purchase Order"; the element is satisfied without it, and adding it is only warranted if an order-level exit is commercially needed.
